entries.label: Elasticity of substitution between capital and labour (long run)
entries.units: elasticity (Δln K per −Δln user cost, output held constant)

citation.authors: Robert S. Chirinko, Steven M. Fazzari and Andrew P. Meyer
citation.title: A New Approach to Estimating Production Function Parameters: The Elusive Capital–Labor Substitution Elasticity

entries.quote: Our results are based on an extensive panel comprising 1860 firms. Our approach generates a precisely estimated elasticity of 0.40.
entries.derivation: Value = the abstract's estimate (0.40). The abstract gives no standard error, so the range is the tool's ±50% rule (F-U-02): 0.20 to 0.60.
entries.notes: Read in the abstract only ([A]); the full text is behind a paywall and the 2004 CESifo working-paper version could not be downloaded. The estimate uses long-run variation in a US firm panel. Treasury's CGE model uses 0.9 (range 0.4 to 1.4) for a different, nested elasticity (entry c3.sigma.kpb2016).

entries.label: Substitution elasticity between labour and non-structures capital in Treasury's CGE model (sensitivity)

citation.authors: Michael Kouparitsas, Dinar Prihardini and Alexander Beames
citation.title: Analysis of the long term effects of a company tax cut
citation.locator: Appendix A, 'Substitutability of capital and labour', p. 36 (PDF p. 39); Table 8, p. 39 (PDF p. 42)

entries.quote: With an elasticity of 0.9, labour and non-structures capital are modelled as gross complements. … In order to test the sensitivity of the results to this elasticity a reasonable empirical range is assumed with a lower bound of 0.4 and an upper bound of 1.4.
entries.derivation: Value = the model's base case (0.9); low and high = the paper's sensitivity bounds (0.4 and 1.4), reported in Table 8.
entries.notes: A calibrated CGE parameter, not an estimate: the paper says the base value "falls within the range of estimates reviewed by Gunning et al. (2007)". It is the elasticity between labour and non-structures capital in a nested production function, which is not the same object as an aggregate capital–labour σ. Kept as a sensitivity, as in the plan (§6.2 C3).

entries.label: Capital share of value added (α), by industry
entries.country: Australia (16 market-sector industries, divisions A to N, R and S)

citation.title: Estimates of Industry Multifactor Productivity, Australia, 2024-25 (5260.0.55.002)
citation.locator: Table 14, 'Capital income shares', row '16 Market sector industries (b)', columns 2015-16 to 2024-25

entries.quote: Table 14: Income Shares for Value Added based Estimates of Multifactor Productivity … Capital income shares … 16 Market sector industries (b)
entries.derivation: Value = the market-sector capital income share in 2024-25 (0.4387, rounded to 0.439). Low and high = its lowest and highest values in the ten years to 2024-25 (0.4036 in 2015-16; 0.4809 in 2022-23).

dataSupplied.table: Table 14, Capital income shares, one row per market-sector division
dataSupplied.note: The engine uses each division's own share from the parameter file; this entry's value is the fallback for an industry with no published share (outside the market sector).

entries.notes: A measured statistic (method "data", interpretation A-P16). Under growth accounting, the income share stands in for the output elasticity of capital, which assumes competitive factor markets and constant returns. Shares vary widely by division (2024-25: Administrative and support services 0.056, Mining 0.817), so the per-industry values matter; the per-industry range is left to the pipeline.
